title: A hymn in Bhairao
hook: Namdev carries a cup of milk to the Lord, and Guru Arjan names the One he serves

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Bhairao, which opens with Guru Nanak's line that nothing happens outside the One. Your line was serious morning. Did the heavy thing feel any different with a breath before it? Day one thousand one hundred thirteen.

A brown cow, a pail, and someone who has been given a job. He milks the cow, pours the milk into a cup, fills a jug with water, and carries both to the Lord. Then he waits for the Lord to drink. That's the opening of a hymn by the Bhagat Namdev, and it sits in the Bhairao section of the Guru Granth Sahib, in his own words. It's this week's last day, so we'll look back too. But first, a cup of milk that somebody expects to be finished.
screen: `A BROWN COW AND A CUP.` → `HE CARRIES IT TO THE LORD.` → `AND WAITS.`

segments.voice: Here's the hymn, in paraphrase. Namdev milks the brown cow and brings the milk in a cup, with water in a jug. He sets it before the Lord and pleads: drink this, Lord, and my mind will be at peace. If you don't, my father at home will be angry. Then the turn. A golden cup, filled with nectar, is set before the Lord, and the hymn has God say that this one devotee lives in his heart, and smile on seeing Namdev. The Lord drinks the milk. The devotee goes home, and Namdev has seen the Lord. Tradition fills in the edges: Namdev was a child, and his father, who usually made the daily offering, had asked him to do it. The hymn itself keeps it simple. A cup, a plea, a smile, an empty cup. What makes it stay with people is Namdev's directness. He doesn't offer the milk as a ritual to be performed and cleared away. He offers it as a gift to someone who is really there, and he means it to be received. The same section holds a hymn of Guru Arjan that speaks of serving only the One who protects in the end, and says body and breath belong to the One who is called both Allah and Ram. Two voices, one point: devotion is offered to someone present. Looking back over this week, from Maru's true warrior through Tukhari's months, Kedara's tender evening and Bhairao's serious morning, each raga has handed over something you could carry. Today it's a cup. Your line: the milk offering.
screen: `MILK IN A CUP, WATER IN A JUG.` · `DRINK, AND MY MIND WILL BE AT PEACE.` · `THE LORD SMILES AND DRINKS.` · `OFFERED TO SOMEONE PRESENT.` · then, large: `THE MILK OFFERING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to one Bhairao shabad, and offer one plain thing. If you can, find a recording of Namdev's milk hymn or another shabad in Bhairao. If not, sit in the quiet. Bring to mind one ordinary thing you'll give today: a meal you'll cook, a message you'll answer, an hour of work. Hold it the way Namdev holds the cup, not as a chore to clear, but as something meant to be received. Breathe slowly around it. If you pray, you can offer it with Waheguru on the breath. If you don't, simply let the giving be wholehearted. The bell holds the time.
A hymn in Bhairao. Namdev's song of the cup of milk he carries to the Lord, pleading for it to be drunk, and the Lord smiling and drinking. Today's word.
Your line: the milk offering. Pick one small thing you hand to someone today, a cup of tea, a reply, a ride, and give it as if you expect it to be received. Day one thousand one hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Namdev's hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib are sung in kirtan alongside the Gurus' own, and the milk hymn in Bhairao is retold with the story of the boy Namdev making the offering.
